questions.prompt: A cyclist speeds up uniformly from 4.0 m s⁻¹ to 10.0 m s⁻¹ while covering 42 m of road. Find the acceleration.
options: a = (v − u) / t
s = ut + ½at²
s = ½(u + v)t
v² = u² + 2as
questions.explanation: You are given u, v and s, and asked for a. Time is neither given nor wanted, so use the one equation that leaves t out. Both a = (v − u)/t and s = ut + ½at² demand a time you do not have, and s = ½(u + v)t would only hand t back to you.

questions.prompt: A stone is released from rest and falls 45 m to the ground. Air resistance is negligible. Find the time it takes to fall.
options: s = ut + ½at²
v² = u² + 2as
v = u + at
s = ½(u + v)t
questions.explanation: Known: u = 0, s = 45 m, a = g. Wanted: t. Only s = ut + ½at² contains those four quantities and nothing else. v² = u² + 2as gives you the landing speed rather than the time, and both v = u + at and s = ½(u + v)t need a value of v you have not worked out yet.

questions.prompt: A 1200 kg car slows uniformly from 20 m s⁻¹ to rest in 5.0 s. Find the average braking force.
options: F_R = ma, on its own
W = Fs, then P = W / t
a = (v − u) / t, then F_R = ma
F_R × s = ½mv² − ½mu²
questions.explanation: F_R = ma is the right finishing move, but on its own it is incomplete — you have no acceleration yet, so find it from the velocities and the time first. The work–energy route would work if you knew the braking distance, but here you were given a time instead.

questions.prompt: A 0.50 kg ball is thrown vertically upward at 12 m s⁻¹. How high does it rise? Air resistance is negligible.
options: v² = u² + 2as, taking v = 0 at the highest point
½mv² = mgh, with the mass cancelling
Either the kinematic route or the energy route — both give the same height
P = Fv, using the weight as the force
questions.explanation: Both routes are valid and both give 7.2 m. The kinematic route uses v = 0 at the highest point; the energy route says the whole kinetic store converts to the gravitational potential store, with the mass cancelling. Recognising that the two must agree is worth more than either one alone.

questions.prompt: A 0.20 kg ball and a 2.0 kg ball are released from rest at the same height, with no air resistance. Which equation shows they must hit the ground at the same speed?
options: F_R = ma
mgh = ½mv², because m cancels from both sides
W = mg
P = Fv
questions.explanation: Write mgh = ½mv² and the mass appears on both sides, so it cancels, leaving v = √(2gh). The landing speed cannot depend on mass. This is the single most reused result in the topic, and none of the force or power equations reveal it.

questions.prompt: An electric motor draws 400 W and lifts a 300 N crate through 8.0 m in 12 s. Find the efficiency of the motor.
options: useful = mgh, total = Fs, then efficiency = useful ÷ total × 100%
P = Fv, then efficiency = useful ÷ total × 100%
P = W / t, on its own
useful = Fs, total = Pt, then efficiency = useful ÷ total × 100%
questions.explanation: The useful output is the work done lifting the crate, Fs = 2400 J. The total input is what the motor drew over that time, Pt = 4800 J, giving 50%. The version built on mgh fails because the mass was never given — and Fs is the useful output, not the input.

questions.prompt: A 1500 kg lift is moving upward at a constant 2.5 m s⁻¹. Find the tension in the cable.
options: F_R = ma with a = 0, together with W = mg
F_R = ma with a = 2.5 m s⁻²
P = Fv
v² = u² + 2as
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means a = 0, so the resultant force is zero and the tension simply equals the weight, 15 000 N. The tempting alternative substitutes 2.5 as an acceleration — but 2.5 m s⁻¹ is a velocity. Check the unit before you substitute.

questions.prompt: A student carries a 40 N bag horizontally for 15 m at a steady walking speed. How much work does the student do against gravity?
options: W = Fs, with s = 15 m
E_P = mgh, with h = 15 m
W = Fs, with s = 0 m, because there is no vertical displacement
P = W / t
questions.explanation: Work counts only the distance moved in the direction of the force. The weight acts downwards while the bag moves sideways, so that distance is zero and the work done against gravity is 0 J — however tired the student feels. Using s = 15 m multiplies the weight by a displacement perpendicular to it.

questions.prompt: A 900 kg car travelling at 30 m s⁻¹ brakes to rest in a distance of 75 m. Find the average braking force using energy.
options: a = (v − u) / t, then F_R = ma
F_R × s = ½mv² − ½mu²
P = Fv
mgh = ½mv²
questions.explanation: The work–energy theorem links a force acting over a distance to the change in the kinetic store, which is exactly the pair of quantities you were given. Going via a = (v − u)/t needs a time that was never stated, and mgh needs a height that does not exist on level ground.

questions.prompt: A skydiver has been falling long enough to reach terminal velocity. Which statement correctly describes her motion at that moment?
options: F_R = ma, with F_R = 0 N and therefore a = 0 m s⁻²
v² = u² + 2as, using a = g
s = ut + ½at², using a = g
F_R = ma, with F_R equal to her weight
questions.explanation: At terminal velocity the air resistance has grown until it equals the weight. The forces balance, so the resultant force is 0 N and the acceleration is 0 m s⁻² — she keeps moving, at a constant velocity. The two equations of motion offered both assume a free fall that stopped being true long ago.

questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg book is lifted 1.5 m onto a shelf at a steady speed. How much work does the lifting force do?
options: W = mg for the lifting force, then W = Fs
F_R = ma with a = 0, so the force is 0 N and no work is done
E_K = ½mv²
P = Fv
questions.explanation: At a steady speed the lifting force balances the weight, so it is mg = 20 N and the work done is 20 × 1.5 = 30 J. The trap is confusing the resultant force, which really is zero, with the lifting force, which certainly is not. A zero resultant force does not mean no work is being done.

questions.prompt: A car of mass 800 kg accelerates from rest to 15 m s⁻¹ over 50 m of level road. Ignoring friction, find the driving force.
options: v² = u² + 2as, then F_R = ma
F_R × s = ½mv² − ½mu²
P = Fv, then W = Fs
Either the kinematic route or the work–energy route — both give 1800 N
questions.explanation: Kinematics gives a = 15² ÷ (2 × 50) = 2.25 m s⁻² and then F = 1800 N. Energy gives the same in one line: the work done, F × 50, equals the 90 kJ gained by the kinetic store. Seeing that the work–energy theorem is really F = ma multiplied through by distance is the point of this one.

questions.prompt: A stone is thrown horizontally from a cliff at 5.0 m s⁻¹ and lands 2.0 s later. Find the height of the cliff. Air resistance is negligible.
options: s = ut + ½at², using only the vertical motion with u = 0
s = ut + ½at², using u = 5.0 m s⁻¹
v² = u² + 2as, using v = 5.0 m s⁻¹
s = ½(u + v)t, using u = v = 5.0 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: Horizontal and vertical motion are completely independent. The 5.0 m s⁻¹ is entirely horizontal and has no effect on how fast the stone falls, so vertically u = 0 and h = ½ × 10 × 2.0² = 20 m. Feeding the horizontal speed into a vertical equation gives 30 m, which is wrong.

questions.prompt: A 500 W motor runs for 2.0 minutes. How much energy does it transfer in that time?
options: E = Pt, with t = 2.0
E = Pt, with t = 120 s
P = Fv
W = Fs
questions.explanation: The watt is a joule per second, so the time must be in seconds: 500 × 120 = 60 000 J. Leaving t in minutes gives 1000 J, a factor of sixty out. Converting units before substituting is the whole question here.

questions.prompt: A 60 kg cyclist freewheels from rest down a hill, dropping 12 m in height. Ignoring friction and air resistance, find the speed at the bottom.
options: mgh = ½mv², with the mass cancelling
v² = u² + 2as, using a = g and s = 12 m
F_R = ma
P = Fv
questions.explanation: Energy handles a slope effortlessly: the drop in the gravitational potential store equals the gain in the kinetic store, so v = √(2gh) = 15.5 m s⁻¹, whatever the shape of the hill. The kinematic version fails because on a slope the acceleration is not g, and the distance travelled is not the 12 m of height.

questions.prompt: A 4.0 kg box slides 3.0 m across a rough floor and stops. The frictional force on it is 5.0 N. How much energy is transferred out of its kinetic store?
options: W = Fs, with F = 5.0 N and s = 3.0 m
W = Fs, with F = the weight, 40 N
E_P = mgh, with h = 3.0 m
F_R = ma
questions.explanation: Only the frictional force does work here, giving 5.0 × 3.0 = 15 J. The weight points straight down while the box moves sideways, so it does no work at all — and there is no change in height, so mgh is zero too.

questions.prompt: Two identical cars, one at 10 m s⁻¹ and one at 20 m s⁻¹, brake with the same force. Which equation shows the faster car needs four times the stopping distance?
options: v = u + at
F_R = ma
F × s = ½mv², so s is proportional to v²
P = Fv
questions.explanation: Rearranged, s = mv² ÷ 2F. With the force and the mass fixed, the stopping distance goes as the square of the speed, so doubling the speed quadruples the distance. This is the single most useful road-safety result in the syllabus.

questions.prompt: A 1200 W kettle is 85% efficient. How much useful energy does it deliver in 90 s?
options: E = Pt, then useful = efficiency × total
efficiency = useful ÷ total, taking useful = Pt
P = Fv
W = Fs
questions.explanation: Pt gives the total energy drawn, 108 kJ. The efficiency then tells you what fraction of that came out usefully: 0.85 × 108 kJ = 91.8 kJ. The trap treats Pt as the useful output, when it is the input.

questions.prompt: A ball is dropped and bounces back to 60% of its original height. Which approach finds the fraction of energy transferred away in the bounce?
options: E_K = ½mv² before the bounce only
Compare mgh before and after — the masses cancel, so the fraction lost is 1 − h₂/h₁
F_R = ma
P = W / t
questions.explanation: Both heights are measured for the same ball, so writing mgh₂ ÷ mgh₁ lets m and g cancel, leaving a pure ratio of heights. The fraction lost is 1 − 0.60 = 40%, and you never need the mass at all.

questions.prompt: A 70 kg athlete runs up a slope, gaining 5.0 m in height, in 8.0 s. Find the useful power output.
options: E_P = mgh, then P = W / t
E_K = ½mv², then P = W / t
W = Fs with s = 5.0 m and F = ma
efficiency = useful ÷ total
questions.explanation: The useful work is raising the athlete's own weight through the vertical height, mgh = 3500 J, and power is that work per second: 3500 ÷ 8.0 = 438 W. No speed is given for a kinetic-store calculation, and the athlete finishes at much the same speed anyway.

questions.prompt: A parachutist opens her chute and slows non-uniformly from 55 m s⁻¹ to a new terminal velocity of 10 m s⁻¹ over 6.0 s. Find the distance she covers during that deceleration.
options: s = ½(u + v)t
v² = u² + 2as
None of the equations of motion — find the area under the velocity–time graph
F_R × s = ½mv² − ½mu²
questions.explanation: Every equation of motion assumes uniform acceleration. Here the air resistance changes every instant, so the acceleration is not uniform and none of them apply. The area under the velocity–time graph always works, uniform or not. The work–energy option fails for the same reason: the resultant force is not constant either.

questions.prompt: A 1000 kg car starts from rest and drives 120 m up a slope inclined at 5.0°, with a constant driving force of 6.0 kN and 800 N of friction. Find its speed at the top.
options: F_R = ma with F_R = 6000 − 800, then v² = u² + 2as
v² = u² + 2as with a = 6000 ÷ 1000
P = Fv, then W = Fs
Fs = mgh + ½mv² + fs, with h = 120 sin 5.0°
questions.explanation: On a slope, part of the weight also acts along the direction of motion, so 6000 − 800 is not the resultant force. Going by energy sidesteps that entirely: the work done by the engine is shared between the gravitational potential store, the kinetic store, and the energy transferred away by friction. This exact error is called out in your Worksheet 9 mark scheme.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upward from the edge of a cliff with speed u, and lands at the base of the cliff with speed 2u. Which route relates the cliff height h to u?
options: v² = u² + 2as, with v = 2u and s = −h
s = ut + ½at²
mgh = ½mv², using v = 2u
½m(2u)² = mgh
questions.explanation: No time is mentioned anywhere, so reach for the equation without t. Taking up as positive: 4u² = u² + 2gh, giving h = 3u²/2g. Both energy options offered quietly forget that the ball already had kinetic energy when it left the hand, so they overestimate the height.

questions.prompt: Two blocks of 3.0 kg and 5.0 kg are joined by a light string on a smooth horizontal surface. A 24 N force pulls the 5.0 kg block. Find the tension in the string.
options: F_R = ma on the whole 8.0 kg system only
F_R = ma on the whole 8.0 kg system, then F_R = ma again on the 3.0 kg block alone
W = Fs applied to each block
F_R = ma on the 5.0 kg block only
questions.explanation: Two applications, in that order. The whole system gives the shared acceleration, 24 ÷ 8.0 = 3.0 m s⁻². Then the 3.0 kg block on its own has only the tension acting on it, so T = 3.0 × 3.0 = 9.0 N. Treating the system as a whole and stopping there makes the tension vanish, because it is an internal force.

questions.prompt: A pendulum bob is released from a height of 10 cm. In the presence of air it swings across and rises to only 8 cm on the far side. Which equation accounts for the missing height?
options: mgh = ½mv²
v² = u² + 2as
mgh₁ = mgh₂ + energy transferred to the internal stores of the bob and the air
F_R = ma
questions.explanation: Energy is never destroyed, only moved somewhere less useful. The 2 cm of lost height corresponds to energy transferred to the internal stores of the bob and the surrounding air by the resistive forces. Setting mgh = ½mv² would only be true if there were no air at all.

questions.prompt: A car covers the first half of a journey at 20 m s⁻¹ and the second half, the same distance again, at 30 m s⁻¹. Find its average speed for the whole journey.
options: average speed = (20 + 30) ÷ 2
average speed = total distance ÷ total time, working out each half's time separately
s = ½(u + v)t
v² = u² + 2as
questions.explanation: The answer is 24 m s⁻¹, not 25. The car spends longer in the slower half, so that half carries more weight. Average speed is only ever total distance over total time. Averaging the two speeds directly, or reaching for s = ½(u + v)t, both quietly assume the halves took equal times — but they covered equal distances.

questions.prompt: A 10.5 g nail is dropped from rest 80.0 cm above a cork board and embeds 4.8 cm into it. Find the average resisting force from the board.
options: mgh with h = 0.800 m, then W = Fd with d = 0.048 m
F_R = ma, using a = g
½mv² with v found from v = gt
mgh with h = 0.848 m, then W = Fd with d = 0.048 m
questions.explanation: The nail keeps falling while it decelerates, so the total drop is 80.0 + 4.8 = 84.8 cm. Using only the 80.0 cm gives 1.75 N instead of the correct 1.86 N. The energy released over the full drop is what the board has to absorb over the 4.8 cm it penetrates.

questions.prompt: A crane raises a 500 kg load at a constant 0.80 m s⁻¹. Find the power the crane is developing.
options: W = mg for the tension, then P = Fv
F_R = ma with a = 0.80 m s⁻²
E_P = mgh, then P = W / t
½mv², then P = W / t
questions.explanation: Constant speed means the tension equals the weight, 5000 N, and P = Fv gives 4000 W. The route through E_P = mgh and P = W/t is sound physics but unusable here — you were given neither a height nor a time. And 0.80 m s⁻¹ is a velocity, not an acceleration.

questions.prompt: A trolley of mass m reaches the bottom of a ramp at speed v, then slides a distance d along a rough horizontal surface before stopping. Find the average frictional force.
options: F_R × s = ½mv² − ½mu², so f = ½mv² ÷ d
mgh = ½mv²
F_R = ma, with a = v ÷ t
P = Fv
questions.explanation: On the rough surface the whole kinetic store is removed by friction acting over distance d, so f × d = ½mv². Using F_R = ma with a = v ÷ t would be fine if you had been given the stopping time — you were given a distance instead, and that is the signal to go via energy.

questions.prompt: Two identical stones are dropped from a tall cliff, the second released 1.0 s after the first. Which approach shows that the gap between them grows as they fall?
options: v² = u² + 2as applied to both
Apply s = ½gt² to each stone separately and subtract the two displacements
The gap stays constant, because both have the same acceleration
F_R = ma applied to both
questions.explanation: Both fall with the same acceleration, but the first stone is always moving faster, so it gains ground every second. Subtracting the two displacements gives a gap of ½g(2t − 1), which grows without limit. The intuition that equal accelerations must mean a constant gap is the one most people have, and it is wrong.

questions.prompt: A lift of total mass 800 kg accelerates upward at 1.5 m s⁻². Find the tension in the cable.
options: Tension = mg only
F_R = ma with F_R = T − mg, together with W = mg
Tension = ma only
P = Fv
questions.explanation: Two forces act on the lift: the tension up and the weight down. Their difference is the resultant force, so T − mg = ma and T = m(g + a) = 9200 N. Using mg alone gives 8000 N, which is the answer for a lift moving at constant speed, not an accelerating one.

questions.prompt: A 0.30 kg ball is dropped from 2.0 m and rebounds to 1.2 m. Find the energy transferred away during the bounce, in joules.
options: mgh before the bounce minus mgh after it
½mv², with v found from v² = 2gh
1 − h₂/h₁, expressed as a percentage
F_R = ma
questions.explanation: The question asks for an amount of energy, so the answer must be in joules, not a ratio: 0.30 × 10 × (2.0 − 1.2) = 2.4 J. The ratio 1 − h₂/h₁ correctly gives 40%, but a percentage is not an answer in joules. Read what the question actually asks for.

questions.prompt: A trolley is pushed with a constant 12 N force across a rough surface at constant velocity for 5.0 m. How much energy is transferred to the internal store of the surroundings?
options: W = Fs with F = 12 N — all of it, since the kinetic store does not change
W = Fs, then subtract ½mv²
F_R = ma
E_P = mgh
questions.explanation: At constant velocity the kinetic store is unchanged from start to finish, so every joule the push delivers, 12 × 5.0 = 60 J, ends up in the internal store of the surfaces and the air. If the trolley had been speeding up, only part of it would have.

questions.prompt: Two masses, 2.0 kg and 3.0 kg, hang from either end of a light string over a frictionless pulley and are released. Find the acceleration of the system.
options: F_R = ma on the system, with F_R = (3.0 − 2.0)g and m = 5.0 kg
F_R = ma on the 3.0 kg mass only
F_R = ma with m = 1.0 kg
mgh = ½mv²
questions.explanation: The resultant force driving the system is the difference in the two weights, (3.0 − 2.0)g = 10 N, but the mass being accelerated is both blocks together, 5.0 kg. That gives a = 2.0 m s⁻². Using the difference in mass for both roles is the classic slip.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m s⁻¹ and caught 4.0 s later at the same height. Find its displacement over the whole flight.
options: s = ut + ½at² over the full 4.0 s, giving 0 m
s = ½(u + v)t with v = 20 m s⁻¹, giving 80 m
Twice the maximum height, giving 40 m
v² = u² + 2as
questions.explanation: Displacement is measured from start to finish, and the ball ends exactly where it began, so it is zero. The 40 m answer is the distance travelled, which is a different quantity. The 80 m answer forgets that the final velocity is −20 m s⁻¹, not +20.

questions.prompt: A car engine delivers 60 kW while the car travels at a constant 25 m s⁻¹ on a level road. Find the total resistive force acting on it.
options: P = Fv for the driving force, and at constant velocity the resistance equals it
P = Fv, then F_R = ma
W = Fs, then P = W / t
E_K = ½mv²
questions.explanation: P = Fv gives the driving force, 60 000 ÷ 25 = 2400 N. Because the velocity is constant, the resultant force is zero, so the resistive forces must exactly balance that driving force at 2400 N. Notice that the mass of the car is never needed.

questions.prompt: A spring-loaded toy launches a 0.050 kg ball vertically to a height of 1.8 m. Find the energy that was stored in the compressed spring.
options: The elastic store converts to the gravitational potential store, so E = mgh
E = ½mv², with v found from v = gt
F_R = ma
W = Fs, with s equal to the spring's compression
questions.explanation: Follow the energy: elastic store → kinetic store at launch → gravitational potential store at the top, where the ball is momentarily at rest. Since the two ends of that chain are equal, E = mgh = 0.9 J. The compression distance is never needed, and was never given.

questions.prompt: A 60 kg skydiver is falling at a constant 50 m s⁻¹. Find the power being dissipated against air resistance.
options: At terminal velocity the air resistance equals the weight, then P = Fv
E_K = ½mv², then P = W / t
E_P = mgh, then P = W / t
W = Fs
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means the air resistance has grown to equal the weight, 600 N, so P = Fv = 600 × 50 = 30 kW. The kinetic store is not changing at all, and no height or time was given, so the other routes have nothing to work with.

questions.prompt: The energy in a car's kinetic store is found to have quadrupled. By what factor has its speed increased?
options: E_K = ½mv², so v is proportional to √E — the speed doubles
E_K = ½mv², so the speed also quadruples
F_R = ma
P = Fv
questions.explanation: Because the energy depends on v², the speed depends on the square root of the energy. Four times the energy means √4 = 2 times the speed. The same square relationship is why stopping distance quadruples when speed doubles.

questions.prompt: A conveyor belt raises 500 kg of sand every minute through a height of 3.0 m. Find the minimum power needed.
options: E_P = mgh for one minute's sand, then P = W / t with t = 60 s
E_P = mgh, then P = W / t with t = 1
P = Fv, with v = 3.0 m s⁻¹
E_K = ½mv²
questions.explanation: Work out the energy for one minute's worth of sand, mgh = 15 000 J, then divide by the 60 seconds it took, giving 250 W. Dividing by 1 treats a minute as a second and inflates the answer sixtyfold. The 3.0 m is a height, not a speed.

questions.prompt: A colourless solution gives a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide, and the precipitate dissolves when the sodium hydroxide is added in excess. Which test tells you whether the cation is Al³⁺ or Zn²⁺?
options: Add aqueous ammonia dropwise until it is in excess
Add dilute nitric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate
Bubble the solution through limewater
Add dilute acid and test the gas with a lighted splint
questions.explanation: Both amphoteric hydroxides dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide, so that test alone cannot separate them. Aqueous ammonia does: Zn(OH)₂ dissolves in excess ammonia, while Al(OH)₃ stays put. The silver nitrate and limewater tests are for anions and gases, not cations.

questions.prompt: You have collected a colourless, odourless gas and suspect it is oxygen. Which test confirms it?
options: Insert a glowing splint — it relights
Place a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube — it goes out with a squeaky pop
Hold moist red litmus paper at the mouth — it turns blue
Bubble it through acidified potassium manganate(VII)
questions.explanation: A glowing splint relighting is the oxygen test. The squeaky pop belongs to hydrogen, moist red litmus turning blue to ammonia, and decolourising potassium manganate(VII) to sulfur dioxide.

questions.prompt: You need to test a solution for chloride ions. Which procedure is correct?
options: Add dilute nitric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate
Add dilute hydrochloric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate
Add dilute nitric acid, then aqueous barium nitrate
Add aqueous sodium hydroxide and warm
questions.explanation: Nitric acid first, to remove carbonate ions that would also give a white precipitate, then silver nitrate for the white AgCl. Using hydrochloric acid would add chloride ions of its own, so you would get a white precipitate no matter what the sample contained. Barium nitrate is the sulfate test.

questions.prompt: Which procedure identifies a carbonate?
options: Add dilute acid and bubble the gas produced through limewater
Add dilute nitric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate
Add aqueous sodium hydroxide and a piece of aluminium foil, then warm
Add dilute nitric acid, then aqueous barium nitrate
questions.explanation: Carbonates effervesce with dilute acid, releasing carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky. The other three are the tests for halides, nitrate and sulfate respectively.

questions.prompt: Which procedure identifies a nitrate?
options: Add aqueous sodium hydroxide and a small piece of aluminium foil, then warm
Add dilute nitric acid, then aqueous silver nitrate
Bubble the gas through limewater
Add aqueous barium nitrate
questions.explanation: The aluminium reduces the nitrate ion to ammonia in the warm alkaline mixture, and the pungent gas turns moist red litmus blue. Adding nitric acid would be self-defeating here — it introduces the very ion you are testing for.

questions.prompt: Which procedure identifies a sulfate?
options: Add dilute nitric acid, then aqueous barium nitrate
Add dilute sulfuric acid, then aqueous barium nitrate
Add aqueous silver nitrate
Add aqueous sodium hydroxide until in excess
questions.explanation: Nitric acid clears out carbonate, then barium nitrate gives the white BaSO₄. Using sulfuric acid pours sulfate ions into the sample, so a white precipitate would appear whatever you started with.

questions.prompt: You need a soluble lead(II) compound as a starting material. Which one dissolves in water?
options: Lead(II) nitrate
Lead(II) chloride
Lead(II) sulfate
Lead(II) carbonate
questions.explanation: All nitrates are soluble, with no exceptions — the N in SPAN. Lead is one of the “Pure Art Courses” exceptions for chlorides and one of the “Sciences” exceptions for sulfates, and carbonates are insoluble unless the cation is Na⁺, K⁺ or NH₄⁺.

questions.prompt: You are asked to prepare barium sulfate, which is insoluble in water. Which method?
options: Precipitation — mix two suitable soluble solutions and filter off the solid
Add excess insoluble base to warm acid, then filter off the excess
Titration using an indicator
Evaporate a solution of it to dryness
questions.explanation: The first question in salt preparation is always “is the salt soluble?” If the answer is no, you precipitate it by mixing two soluble solutions that between them supply the right ions, then filter, wash and dry.

questions.prompt: You need to prepare copper(II) sulfate, a soluble salt that contains neither a Group 1 metal nor ammonium. Which method?
options: Add excess copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid, then filter off the unreacted excess
Mix aqueous copper(II) nitrate with aqueous sodium sulfate and filter
Titrate dilute sulfuric acid against aqueous sodium hydroxide
Add copper metal to warm dilute sulfuric acid
questions.explanation: Excess insoluble base plus acid, then filtration — the excess solid tells you the acid is used up, and it filters straight out. Copper metal will not work at all, because copper sits below hydrogen in the reactivity series and does not displace it from acids.

questions.prompt: You need to prepare sodium chloride, a soluble salt containing a Group 1 metal. Which method?
options: Titration — find the exact volumes with an indicator, then repeat without it
Add excess sodium hydroxide to hydrochloric acid, then filter
Mix two soluble solutions and filter off the precipitate
Add sodium metal to dilute hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Every reactant here is soluble, so there is no leftover solid to filter off — that rules the filtration method out. Titration finds the exact volumes that react, and the run is then repeated without indicator so the product is not contaminated.

questions.prompt: Which indicator is the usual choice for a titration involving a strong acid?
options: Methyl orange
Phenolphthalein
Universal indicator
Bromothymol blue
questions.explanation: Methyl orange changes over pH 3.1 to 4.4, which sits in the right region for a strong acid. Phenolphthalein, changing over pH 8.3 to 10.0, is the partner choice for titrations of weak acids.

questions.prompt: You want to estimate the actual pH value of a solution, not just whether it is acidic or alkaline. Which indicator?
options: Universal indicator
Litmus
Methyl orange
Phenolphthalein
questions.explanation: Universal indicator runs continuously from 0 to 14, red through green to purple, so it reads a value. The others flip between two colours at a single narrow range, which tells you which side of that range you are on and nothing more.

questions.prompt: A colourless, pungent gas turns moist red litmus paper blue. Which gas is it?
options: Ammonia
Chlorine
Sulfur dioxide
Hydrogen
questions.explanation: Turning moist red litmus blue means the gas is alkaline, and ammonia is the only alkaline gas in the syllabus. Chlorine turns moist blue litmus red and then bleaches it, and it is yellow-green rather than colourless.

questions.prompt: Which test confirms that a gas is hydrogen?
options: Place a lighted splint at the mouth of the tube — the gas burns with a squeaky pop
Insert a glowing splint — it relights
Bubble it through limewater — a white precipitate forms
Hold moist blue litmus at the mouth — it turns red
questions.explanation: Note that it is a lighted splint for hydrogen and a glowing splint for oxygen. Mixing those two up is one of the most common slips in the whole topic.

questions.prompt: Two solutions each give a coloured precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide: one green, one light blue. Both are insoluble in excess. Which is which?
options: Green is Fe²⁺ and light blue is Cu²⁺
Green is Cu²⁺ and light blue is Fe²⁺
Both are Fe³⁺
You cannot tell without adding aqueous ammonia as well
questions.explanation: Green Fe(OH)₂ for iron(II) and light blue Cu(OH)₂ for copper(II). Iron(III) is the third coloured one, giving a red-brown Fe(OH)₃. All three are insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide, so the colour alone is enough.

questions.prompt: A solution gives a red-brown precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide that does not dissolve in excess. Which cation is present?
options: Fe³⁺
Fe²⁺
Cu²⁺
Al³⁺
questions.explanation: Red-brown Fe(OH)₃ is iron(III). Iron(II) gives green, copper(II) gives light blue, and aluminium gives a white precipitate that would dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide.

questions.prompt: A solution produces no precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide, but on warming gives off a colourless pungent gas. Which ion is present, and what confirms it?
options: Ammonium — the gas turns moist red litmus paper blue
Calcium — the gas turns limewater milky
Zinc — the gas relights a glowing splint
Nitrate — the gas burns with a squeaky pop
questions.explanation: No precipitate at all, plus a pungent gas on warming, points to ammonium. The gas is ammonia, so moist red litmus turning blue is the confirmation. Calcium would have given a white precipitate rather than a gas.

questions.prompt: Why is dilute nitric acid added before aqueous silver nitrate when testing for chloride?
options: To remove carbonate ions, which would otherwise give their own white precipitate
To make the solution more concentrated so the precipitate shows up
To speed the reaction up
To help the silver nitrate dissolve
questions.explanation: Silver carbonate is also a white precipitate, so a carbonate in the sample would give a false positive. The acid destroys any carbonate first, as carbon dioxide, leaving only a genuine halide to react.

questions.prompt: You need to prepare zinc chloride, a soluble salt with neither a Group 1 metal nor ammonium. Which combination?
options: Excess zinc oxide added to warm dilute hydrochloric acid, then filtered
Aqueous zinc nitrate mixed with aqueous sodium chloride
Titration of hydrochloric acid against aqueous zinc hydroxide
Zinc oxide added to dilute sulfuric acid
questions.explanation: Soluble salt, no Group 1 or ammonium, so the filtration method applies: excess insoluble base into warm acid, then filter the leftover solid away. The acid must supply the right anion, which means hydrochloric acid for a chloride.

questions.prompt: Which observation identifies chlorine gas?
options: A yellow-green pungent gas turns moist blue litmus paper red, then bleaches it white
A colourless pungent gas turns moist red litmus paper blue
A colourless odourless gas turns limewater milky
A colourless odourless gas relights a glowing splint
questions.explanation: Chlorine is the only coloured gas on the list, and the bleaching step is what clinches it — an acidic gas alone would turn blue litmus red and stop there.

questions.prompt: A solution gives a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess. With aqueous ammonia it also gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia. Which cation is present?
options: Zn²⁺
Al³⁺
Ca²⁺
Either Zn²⁺ or Al³⁺ — these tests cannot separate them
questions.explanation: Both are amphoteric, so both dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide. Only zinc goes on to dissolve in excess ammonia as well, because it forms a soluble complex. Aluminium hydroxide stays as a white solid in excess ammonia.

questions.prompt: A solution gives a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide that stays put in excess, and gives no precipitate at all with aqueous ammonia. Which cation is present?
options: Ca²⁺
Al³⁺
Zn²⁺
NH₄⁺
questions.explanation: Calcium is the white precipitate that is insoluble in excess sodium hydroxide and gives nothing with ammonia. Aluminium and zinc would both have dissolved in excess sodium hydroxide, and ammonium gives no precipitate with either reagent.

questions.prompt: A student tests for sulfate by adding dilute sulfuric acid followed by aqueous barium nitrate, and reports a positive result. What is wrong with the method?
options: The sulfuric acid adds sulfate ions, so a white precipitate forms whatever the sample contained
Barium nitrate is the wrong reagent for sulfate
The acid should have been added after the barium nitrate
Nothing — the method is correct
questions.explanation: The acid is meant to be a spectator that clears out interfering carbonate. Sulfuric acid cannot play that role in a sulfate test because it supplies the ion under investigation. Dilute nitric acid is the neutral choice for both the halide and sulfate tests.

questions.prompt: You are asked to prepare lead(II) chloride. Which method is appropriate, and why?
options: Precipitation, because lead(II) chloride is insoluble — mix aqueous lead(II) nitrate with a soluble chloride and filter
Filtration, adding excess lead(II) oxide to dilute hydrochloric acid
Titration against dilute hydrochloric acid using methyl orange
Adding lead metal to dilute hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Lead is one of the “Pure Art Courses” chloride exceptions, so PbCl₂ is insoluble and precipitation is the route. The filtration method fails here for a subtle reason: the product itself is insoluble, so it would come out of solution mixed in with the unreacted excess solid.

questions.prompt: Why is the titration method, rather than the filtration method, used to prepare potassium nitrate?
options: Every reactant is soluble, so there is no excess solid that could be filtered off
Potassium nitrate is insoluble, so it must be filtered from the mixture
Titration is faster than filtration
Potassium reacts too violently with acids
questions.explanation: The filtration method works precisely because an insoluble excess can be added and then removed. Potassium hydroxide and nitric acid are both soluble, so adding an excess would simply contaminate the product. Titration finds the exact volumes instead.

questions.prompt: A colourless pungent gas turns acidified potassium manganate(VII) from purple to colourless. Which gas is it?
options: Sulfur dioxide
Carbon dioxide
Ammonia
Chlorine
questions.explanation: Decolourising acidified potassium manganate(VII) is the sulfur dioxide test. Carbon dioxide is odourless and does nothing to it, ammonia is alkaline, and chlorine is yellow-green rather than colourless.

questions.prompt: Two colourless gases both turn limewater milky. Which further test separates carbon dioxide from sulfur dioxide?
options: Bubble each through acidified potassium manganate(VII) — only sulfur dioxide decolourises it
Test each with a glowing splint — only carbon dioxide relights it
Hold moist red litmus in each — only carbon dioxide turns it blue
Bubble each through limewater again for longer
questions.explanation: Both are acidic gases and both give the milky limewater result, so limewater cannot separate them. Sulfur dioxide is a reducing agent and decolourises acidified potassium manganate(VII); carbon dioxide is not and leaves it purple. Their smell differs too — pungent against odourless.

questions.prompt: Which pair of solutions, when mixed, will produce a precipitate?
options: Aqueous barium nitrate and aqueous sodium sulfate
Aqueous sodium chloride and aqueous potassium nitrate
Aqueous ammonium carbonate and aqueous sodium hydroxide
Aqueous potassium sulfate and aqueous sodium nitrate
questions.explanation: Work out every possible pairing and check it against the rules. Barium and sulfate meet to give BaSO₄, one of the “Sciences” exceptions, so it drops out as a white solid. In the other three, every ion pairing lands on a soluble compound — all the SPAN cations and nitrates stay dissolved.

questions.prompt: Which of these carbonates will NOT dissolve in water?
options: Calcium carbonate
Sodium carbonate
Ammonium carbonate
Potassium carbonate
questions.explanation: Carbonates are insoluble except when the cation is Na⁺, K⁺ or NH₄⁺ — the SPA crew. Calcium is not in that group, which is why calcium carbonate is a favourite excess reactant for the filtration method.

questions.prompt: Lead is above hydrogen in the reactivity series, yet it barely reacts with dilute sulfuric acid. Why?
options: An insoluble layer of lead(II) sulfate forms and coats the metal, stopping the reaction
Lead is actually below hydrogen, so no reaction is possible
Sulfuric acid is too weak to react with any metal
Lead(II) sulfate is soluble and washes the surface clean
questions.explanation: Lead is one of the “Sciences” sulfate exceptions, so PbSO₄ is insoluble. It forms immediately on the surface and seals the metal off from the acid. This is a neat case of a solubility rule explaining a reactivity observation.

questions.prompt: A white precipitate forms when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a solution, and it dissolves when the mixture is warmed. Which cation is present?
options: Pb²⁺
Ag⁺
Ba²⁺
Ca²⁺
questions.explanation: Lead(II) chloride is insoluble in cold water but dissolves in hot — the redissolving on warming is the giveaway. Silver chloride would also give a white precipitate, but it stays put when warmed.

questions.prompt: Which hydroxide is soluble in water?
options: Barium hydroxide
Copper(II) hydroxide
Iron(III) hydroxide
Zinc hydroxide
questions.explanation: Hydroxides are insoluble except for Na⁺, K⁺ and Ba²⁺. Note that ammonium does not appear on this particular exception list — barium takes its place. The other three are exactly the coloured precipitates you meet in the cation tests.

questions.prompt: You need to prepare ammonium sulfate. Which method applies?
options: Titration, because ammonium salts are made from fully soluble reactants
Filtration, adding excess ammonium carbonate to sulfuric acid
Precipitation, mixing two soluble solutions
Adding ammonia gas directly to solid sulfur
questions.explanation: Ammonium behaves like a Group 1 cation in the salt-preparation decision tree: its salts are soluble and so are its starting materials, so there is nothing insoluble to filter. That leaves titration.

questions.prompt: A weak acid is titrated against a strong base. Which indicator gives the sharpest end point?
options: Phenolphthalein
Methyl orange
Universal indicator
Litmus
questions.explanation: The end point of a weak acid against a strong base falls on the alkaline side, so you want an indicator that changes there. Phenolphthalein switches over pH 8.3 to 10.0, colourless to pink. Methyl orange changes far too early, in the acidic range.

questions.prompt: Why is universal indicator unsuitable for a titration?
options: It changes colour gradually across the whole pH range, so there is no sharp end point
It is not affected by acids
It only works in alkaline solutions
Its colour change cannot be reversed
questions.explanation: A titration needs a single drop to flip the colour decisively. Universal indicator shades continuously from red through green to purple, which is exactly what makes it good for estimating a pH value and useless for spotting an end point.

questions.prompt: Which metal will NOT produce hydrogen when added to dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: Copper
Magnesium
Zinc
Iron
questions.explanation: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series displace it from an acid. Magnesium, zinc and iron all sit above it and fizz. Copper sits below, which is also why copper(II) sulfate has to be made from copper(II) oxide rather than the metal.

questions.prompt: A colourless solution gives no precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide and no gas when warmed with it. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The cation is probably a Group 1 ion such as Na⁺ or K⁺, which form no hydroxide precipitate
The cation must be ammonium
The cation must be calcium
The test has failed and must be repeated
questions.explanation: Sodium and potassium hydroxides are soluble, so no precipitate can form — a negative result is itself informative. Ammonium is ruled out because it would have given a pungent gas on warming, and calcium would have given a white precipitate.

questions.prompt: A student adds a large volume of aqueous sodium hydroxide to an unknown solution all at once, instead of dropwise. What might they miss?
options: An amphoteric hydroxide such as Al(OH)₃ or Zn(OH)₂ would dissolve again before the initial precipitate was ever seen
Nothing — the final result is the same either way
The solution would become too dilute to react
The precipitate would form but change colour
questions.explanation: The whole point of adding dropwise, then to excess is that it gives you two observations rather than one. Flood the tube straight away and an amphoteric hydroxide redissolves instantly, so you record “no precipitate” and wrongly rule out aluminium and zinc.

questions.prompt: A green solid effervesces with dilute nitric acid, giving a gas that turns limewater milky. The resulting solution gives a light blue precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide, insoluble in excess. What was the solid?
options: Copper(II) carbonate
Calcium carbonate
Zinc carbonate
Iron(II) carbonate
questions.explanation: Two deductions, combined. Effervescence with acid plus milky limewater means a carbonate. A light blue hydroxide precipitate that stays put in excess means copper(II). Iron(II) would have been green, calcium and zinc white.

questions.prompt: An unknown solution gives a white precipitate with aqueous silver nitrate after acidification, and a white precipitate with aqueous barium nitrate after acidification. What can you conclude?
options: Both a halide and a sulfate are present — the two tests are independent of each other
Only a sulfate is present; silver sulfate caused the first precipitate
Only a chloride is present; barium chloride caused the second precipitate
The results contradict each other, so the sample is contaminated
questions.explanation: Nothing stops a solution containing more than one anion. Because both tests were acidified first, carbonate interference is already excluded, and each reagent is specific to its own ion. Two positives simply mean two anions.
